One Big, One Small

September 23, 2026

Hello my name is Avi. To learn more about me, please check the root domain. As a reminder, my theme is Art Deco.

For this project, I wanted to try something big. From the start, I always had the idea of creating a small version of a well known Art Deco building, and for this project I finally made an attempt at it. This was heavily inspired by Chris Hytha’s Art Deco building lamps. Chris is an acquaintance and one of the most important voices in advocating for the resurgence of Art Deco-style architecture in America.

I did a good amount of research and looked at about 60 different buildings to see what would be best, and ultimately settled on the Eastern Columbia building in Los Angeles:

Here is me scouting another building, the American Radiator Building, in person.

This project was heavily assisted by Codex. Lots of research into publicly available architectural plans, modifications to parts of the Illustrator file when I was too lazy (e.g., changing everything to a certain color scale), and general back and forth over the scope of the project was super useful here. Codex also helped me decide on beveled corners.

Below was the original Illustrator file I had, which after consulting with various shop staff, I decided was too complex. This was a brutal realization given the amount of time I had spent working on the design of these files. This conversation also helped me realize that much of the implementation complexity was realted to the specific laser cutting machine as opposed to the creation of the Illustrator file.

I then proceeded to remove about 85% of the complexity in the creation of new files. These new files represented a much more “minimalist” representation of the Eastern Columbia building.

However, speaking to Phil breathed some life back into me: evidently, the fire risk of engraving is much lower than cutting. This meant that I could use my original, detailed file. So I converted that file to greyscale and started the engraving process. The result was slightly off to the right (I shifted it too far!), but overall the result was was directionally correct and all the motivation I needed to keep going.

After speaking to Phil again, he apprised me of the speed / depth tradeoff, which is very intuitive: the higher the speed, the shallower the depth. This axiom is especially true for hard materials, which wood is one of. So I cut the speed to 50% and the engravings became very clear, although still quite shallow. Time-permitting, I may have set the laser cutter to operate at 10% speed and 1200 DPI, for each of the eight slabs, but time was not a luxury I possessed. Throughout the process, I experimented with cutting down DPI and speed to very low amounts, which I found worked very well for the smaller slabs. I eventually settled on 300dpi / 13% speed / 100% power for the small slabs, which produced very satisfiyingly deep cuts. You can actually see me dialing in the settings in realtime over time just by looking at different panels:

And these are the larger panels:

Following this, I needed to bezel the sides, which meant 16 cuts from the miter saw in total, which essentially no room for error. I had some time inbetween cuts as I felt that others should use the FusionPro. There was also an impromptu birthday party for a fellow student that I attended. Anyway, in this waiting process, I learned how to angle the miter saw to 45˚ and did one cut semi-sucessfully. The issue with this cut is that it’s a bit difficult to stabilize blocks of wood with clamps. Another issue was that the wood, while looking good to the eye, was actually super warped to begin with.

All this meant that there was always a risk of cutting off parts of the wood that I didn’t intend to, which happened on the first cut. Then, on the third cut, at 9:45, I made the mistake of cutting the wrong side of a slab of wood. I thus decided it was not worth it to hastily operate a miter saw and concluded activities for the night.

The complete vision, which I had all the parts for, was as follows:

Two buildings, comprised of four side panels and two top panels. The side panels would be joined on their bezeled sides. On the bottom panel would sit a large tea light, and light would show through the top layers of windows. Directionally, it would look like this lamp from Chris Hytha, but with wood engravings and the panels would not actually be set back.

I got close. Excited for the next class.
